slides.title: Ordinary Differential Equations

slides.html:
Two Points of View

  • Analytic: the equation is something to "solve"; the goal is a formula
  • Geometric: the equation is a vector field; solutions are curves flowing along it; the shape of orbits and long-run behaviour matter

Most equations have no elementary formula — so the geometric view is the protagonist.
slides.title: Two Points of View

slides.html: 1–2. Concepts and First-Order Equations
slides.title: 1–2. Concepts and First-Order Equations

slides.html:
Classification

Criterion Types
highest derivative first, second, …, n-th order
how terms combine linear / nonlinear
number of independent variables ODE / PDE
explicit dependence non-autonomous / autonomous y'=f(y)

"Linear homogeneous" (g\equiv0) ≠ "homogeneous-type first order" (y'=F(y/x)).
slides.title: Classification

slides.html:
Separation of Variables

y'=g(x)h(y)\ \Rightarrow\ \int\frac{dy}{h(y)}=\int g\,dx+C
  • dividing by h(y) loses constant solutions: check h(c)=0
  • y'=-6xy,\ y(0)=7\Rightarrow y=7e^{-3x^2}
  • y'=\dfrac{4-2x}{3y^2-5},\ y(1)=3\Rightarrow y^3-5y=4x-x^2+9
slides.title: Separation of Variables

slides.html:
First-Order Linear: Integrating Factor

y'+Py=Q,\quad\mu=e^{\int P},\quad(\mu y)'=\mu Q
y=\frac1\mu\Big[C+\int\mu Q\,dx\Big]
  • y'-y=\tfrac{11}8e^{-x/3},\ y(0)=-1\Rightarrow y=-\tfrac{33}{32}e^{-x/3}+\tfrac1{32}e^x
  • x^2y'+xy=\sin x\Rightarrow y=\dfrac1x\Big[y_0+\displaystyle\int_1^x\frac{\sin t}t dt\Big] (keep the non-elementary integral)
slides.title: First-Order Linear: Integrating Factor

slides.html:
Homogeneous-Type and Bernoulli

  • Homogeneous-type y'=F(y/x): v=y/x\Rightarrow xv'=F(v)-v
    • 2xyy'=4x^2+3y^2\Rightarrow y^2=x^2(Cx-4)
  • Bernoulli y'+Py=Qy^n: v=y^{1-n}\Rightarrow v'+(1-n)Pv=(1-n)Q
    • xy'+6y=3xy^{4/3}\Rightarrow y=(x+Cx^2)^{-3}, and also y\equiv0

xy'=y+\sqrt{x^2-y^2}: y=x\sin\ln(x/x_0) holds only for |\ln(x/x_0)|\le\pi/2.
slides.title: Homogeneous-Type and Bernoulli

slides.html:
Exact Equations and Riccati

  • M\,dx+N\,dy=0 is exact ⟺ there is F with F_x=M,F_y=N; M_y=N_x suffices on a rectangle / simply connected set
  • construction: F=\int M\,dx+g(y), find g from F_y=N
  • (6xy-y^3)dx+(4y+3x^2-3xy^2)dy=0\Rightarrow3x^2y-xy^3+2y^2=C
  • Riccati: given a particular solution \tilde y, y=\tilde y+1/v ⟹ v'+(2A\tilde y+B)v=-A
slides.title: Exact Equations and Riccati

slides.html: 3. Existence and Uniqueness
slides.title: 3. Existence and Uniqueness

slides.html:
Local Existence and Uniqueness

f continuous and locally Lipschitz in y (e.g. f,f_y continuous) ⟹ the initial value problem has a unique solution near x_0.

  • first-order linear: P,Q continuous on I ⟹ unique on all of I
  • hypotheses fail ⟹ "the theorem cannot be applied", not "no solution / non-unique"
  • continuity alone does not give uniqueness
slides.title: Local Existence and Uniqueness

slides.html:
More Counterexamples; Singular Solutions

  • y'=1/x,\ y(0)=0: undefined at the initial point, no solution
  • xy'=2y: y(0)=b\ne0 has no solution; for y(0)=0, y=ax^2\,(x\le0),\ bx^2\,(x\ge0) is not unique
  • Clairaut y=xy'-\tfrac14y'^2: p'=0 gives the lines y=Cx-C^2/4; p=2x gives y=x^2
slides.title: More Counterexamples; Singular Solutions

slides.html: 4–5. Second- and Higher-Order Linear Equations
slides.title: 4–5. Second- and Higher-Order Linear Equations

slides.html:
Structure of the Solution Space

y''+py'+qy=f
  • existence–uniqueness: p,q,f continuous ⟹ on all of I
  • superposition: y_h=c_1y_1+c_2y_2, y=y_h+y_p
  • Wronskian W=y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2 (signed): for solutions of one equation, independent ⟺ W\ne0 at a point ⟺ W\ne0 everywhere
  • examples: W(\cos,\sin)=1, W(e^x,xe^x)=e^{2x}
slides.title: Structure of the Solution Space

slides.html:
Undetermined Coefficients

f=e^{\alpha x}[P_m\cos\beta x+Q_m\sin\beta x], try y_p=x^se^{\alpha x}[A_m\cos\beta x+B_m\sin\beta x]

  • s = multiplicity of \alpha+i\beta as a characteristic root (resonance)
  • y''+4y=3x^3\Rightarrow y_p=\tfrac34x^3-\tfrac98x
  • y''-2ry'+r^2y=(2x-3)e^{rx}\Rightarrow y_p=e^{rx}(\tfrac13x^3-\tfrac32x^2)
  • superposition: L[y_1+y_2]=f_1+f_2
slides.title: Undetermined Coefficients

slides.html:
Variation of Constants

y_p=-y_1\!\int\!\frac{y_2f}W\,dx+y_2\!\int\!\frac{y_1f}W\,dx
  • derivation: u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0,\ u_1'y_1'+u_2'y_2'=f
  • W is signed; normalise first if the leading coefficient is not 1
  • works for any continuous f
slides.title: Variation of Constants

slides.html:
Higher-Order Constant Coefficients

L(D)y=0 with characteristic polynomial P(r):

  • real root r (multiplicity m): e^{rx},xe^{rx},\dots,x^{m-1}e^{rx}
  • \alpha\pm i\beta (each multiplicity m): x^ke^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x,\ x^ke^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x
  • 9y^{(5)}-6y^{(4)}+y^{(3)}=0: r^3(3r-1)^2\Rightarrow c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2+(c_3+c_4x)e^{x/3}
  • y^{(4)}+4y=0: roots \pm1\pm i
slides.title: Higher-Order Constant Coefficients

slides.html: 6. Linear Systems and the Matrix Exponential
slides.title: 6. Linear Systems and the Matrix Exponential

slides.html:
Higher-Order Equation → System

x''=f(t,x,x')\ \Rightarrow\ x_1'=x_2,\ x_2'=f(t,x_1,x_2)
  • X'=A(t)X+F(t): A,F continuous ⟹ unique on all of I
  • X=X_h+X_p; the determinant of homogeneous solutions is non-zero at one point iff everywhere
  • equilibria: \det A\ne0 only the origin; rank 1 a line; A=0 the whole plane
slides.title: Higher-Order Equation → System

slides.html:
Solving by Eigenvalues

Av=\lambda v\Rightarrow X=e^{\lambda t}v

  • distinct reals: c_1e^{\lambda_1t}v_1+c_2e^{\lambda_2t}v_2
  • complex \alpha+i\beta,\ v=p+iq: X_1=e^{\alpha t}(p\cos\beta t-q\sin\beta t), X_2=e^{\alpha t}(p\sin\beta t+q\cos\beta t)
  • double root, one eigenvector: X_2=e^{\lambda t}(tv_1+v_2), (A-\lambda I)v_2=v_1
slides.title: Solving by Eigenvalues

slides.html:
Example: an Initial Value Problem

X'=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}X,\ X(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}

eigenvalues -2,5, vectors (1,-3)^T,(2,1)^T; c_1=\tfrac37,\ c_2=\tfrac27:

X=\tfrac37e^{-2t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\end{pmatrix}+\tfrac27e^{5t}\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}
slides.title: Example: an Initial Value Problem

slides.html:
Fundamental Matrix and Matrix Exponential

e^{tA}=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!},\qquad X(t)=e^{(t-t_0)A}X_0
  • \Phi'=A\Phi, X=\Phi(t)\Phi(t_0)^{-1}X_0
  • AB=BA\Rightarrow e^{A+B}=e^Ae^B (commutation required)
  • B=T^{-1}AT\Rightarrow e^B=T^{-1}e^AT
  • A=\lambda I+N,\ N^2=0: e^{tA}=e^{\lambda t}(I+tN)
slides.title: Fundamental Matrix and Matrix Exponential

slides.html:
Generalised Eigenvector Chains

(A-\lambda I)v_1=0,\ (A-\lambda I)v_j=v_{j-1}

X_j=e^{\lambda t}\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}\frac{t^k}{k!}v_{j-k}
  • the factorial denominators cannot be dropped
  • stable subspace E^s (\mathrm{Re}<0), unstable subspace E^u; hyperbolic: \mathbb R^n=E^s\oplus E^u
  • 3-D example \lambda=2,1,-1: a stable line plus an unstable plane
slides.title: Generalised Eigenvector Chains

slides.html: 7–8. Phase Portraits and Conjugacy
slides.title: 7–8. Phase Portraits and Conjugacy
Phase Portraits of Planar Linear Systems

slides.html:
Classification by Eigenvalues

Eigenvalues Portrait Stability
two negative reals stable node asymptotically stable
two positive reals unstable node unstable
one of each sign saddle unstable
\alpha\pm i\beta,\alpha<0 stable spiral asymptotically stable
\alpha\pm i\beta,\alpha>0 unstable spiral unstable
\pm i\beta centre stable, not asymptotically

Double root: star (two eigenvectors) / degenerate (one). Treat zero eigenvalues separately.
slides.title: Classification by Eigenvalues

slides.html:
Change of Coordinates and Rotation

  • X=TY\Rightarrow Y'=T^{-1}ATY: analyse in standard coordinates, map back
  • e^{tB}=e^{\alpha t}\begin{pmatrix}\cos\beta t&\sin\beta t\\-\sin\beta t&\cos\beta t\end{pmatrix}, B=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\-\beta&\alpha\end{pmatrix}
  • \beta>0 clockwise; a linear map may flip orientation — test at a point
  • x'=y,\ y'=-4x: 4x^2+y^2=C, period \pi
slides.title: Change of Coordinates and Rotation

slides.html:
Flows and Topological Conjugacy

H\circ\varphi_t^A=\varphi_t^B\circ H\quad(\forall t)

A homeomorphism H keeping the same time parameter; stronger than orbit equivalence.

  • flow: \varphi_t=e^{tA}, \varphi_{t+s}=\varphi_t\circ\varphi_s
  • 1-D: H(x)=\mathrm{sgn}(x)|x|^{\lambda_2/\lambda_1}; for p\ne1 not a diffeomorphism at the origin
  • similarity: Te^{tB}=e^{tA}T
slides.title: Flows and Topological Conjugacy

slides.html:
Classification of Hyperbolic Systems

Theorem: hyperbolic linear systems of the same dimension are topologically conjugate ⟺ their stable subspaces have the same dimension.

Only three planar classes: sinks (stable dimension 2), saddles (1), sources (0).

A stable node and a stable spiral look different but are topologically the same sink.

Construction: the time to reach the unit circle \tau(x)=-\ln\|x\|/\alpha, H=\varphi^A_{-\tau}\circ\varphi^B_\tau.
slides.title: Classification of Hyperbolic Systems

slides.html: 9–10. One Dimension and Bifurcations
slides.title: 9–10. One Dimension and Bifurcations

slides.html:
Stability Definitions and the Phase Line

  • Lyapunov stable: \forall\varepsilon\,\exists\delta: \|X(0)-X_*\|<\delta\Rightarrow\|X(t)-X_*\|<\varepsilon,\ \forall t\ge0
  • asymptotically stable: stable + nearby solutions converge
  • phase line: f>0 moves right, f<0 left; arrows in from both sides ⟹ stable; in from one side only ⟹ semi-stable (still unstable)
  • f'(c)<0 asymptotically stable, >0 unstable, =0 needs more work
slides.title: Stability Definitions and the Phase Line

slides.html:
Extinction Time

for 0<x_0<H:

t_{\mathrm{ext}}=\frac1{k(N-H)}\ln\frac{H(N-x_0)}{N(H-x_0)}
  • from \dfrac{x-N}{x-H}=Ce^{-q t}, q=k(N-H), C=\dfrac{x_0-N}{x_0-H}
  • the time to reach x=0, not a blow-up where a denominator vanishes
slides.title: Extinction Time

slides.html: 11. Nonlinear Systems
slides.title: 11. Nonlinear Systems

slides.html:
Local Analysis Recipe

  1. equilibria: f=g=0
  2. Jacobian J=\begin{pmatrix}f_x&f_y\\g_x&g_y\end{pmatrix}
  3. eigenvalues at each equilibrium ⟹ type and stability
  4. nullclines, vector field, conserved quantities, polar coordinates
  5. with parameters: find bifurcation values
\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}'=J\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}+R(u,v),\quad\frac{\|R\|}{\|(u,v)\|}\to0
slides.title: Local Analysis Recipe

slides.html:
The Linearisation Criterion

  • all real parts <0: locally asymptotically stable
  • some real part >0: unstable
  • zero real part and none positive: linearisation cannot decide
  • hyperbolic equilibrium: locally topologically the same as the linearisation (Hartman–Grobman)
  • a linearised centre ⇏ a centre of the original system
slides.title: The Linearisation Criterion

slides.html:
A Map of Methods

Problem Method
separable separation of variables (check constants)
linear integrating factor
y'=F(y/x) / Bernoulli v=y/x / v=y^{1-n}
exact M_y=N_x (domain condition)
linear, constant coefficients characteristic roots; undetermined coefficients (resonance); variation of constants
X'=AX eigenvalues, matrix exponential, trace–determinant
nonlinear equilibria → Jacobian → classify → bifurcation
slides.title: A Map of Methods

slides.html:
Four Common Pitfalls

  1. separating variables loses constant solutions
  2. "hypotheses fail" ≠ "no solution / non-unique"
  3. linearisation is reliable only at hyperbolic equilibria
  4. repeated eigenvalues need generalised eigenvectors; the t^k terms carry 1/k!
slides.title: Four Common Pitfalls
